Fenwick Instrument Repairs spent six weeks trialling a shared bench schedule. Its manager, Priya Vale, describes what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful and what Vale would change. The workshop's own summary shows what the trial established – and what it left unmeasured.

By Thomas Barregren

Before the trial, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of one shared bench schedule. It chose Benchline after checking that the software could tell those two statuses apart.

## Fenwick defined its own job statuses

Benchline configured the workshop's choices, including who would update each status, and trained four staff in one online session. The team went on discussing collection arrangements with customers by telephone.

Asked in an email interview with Benchline what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, workshop manager Priya Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

# Fenwick's bench schedule shows which instruments await parts

Fenwick Instrument Repairs spent six weeks trialling a shared bench schedule. Its manager, Priya Vale, describes what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful and what Vale would change. The workshop's own summary shows what the trial established – and what it left unmeasured.

By Thomas Barregren

Before the trial, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, which services brass and woodwind instruments. In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of one shared bench schedule. It chose Benchline after checking that the software could tell those two statuses apart.

## Fenwick defined its own job statuses

Benchline configured the workshop's choices, including who would update each status, and trained four staff in one online session. The team went on discussing collection arrangements with customers by telephone.

Asked in an email interview with Benchline what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, workshop manager Priya Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'

## The summary leaves repair speed unmeasured

The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. With the interview, it records the team's reported experience rather than a recommendation for every workshop.

## Vale looks ahead to the backlog

Vale approved continued use for new jobs but held back the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions. Asked whether the same choice would be made again, and what would change, Vale wrote: 'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'

A manager planning a similar trial can start with the question Fenwick had to settle: what does 'ready for work' mean in your workshop?
EOF

| # | Draft passage | Source passage | Difference / test | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title: "Fenwick staff could see which instruments awaited parts" | "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed" | Whose assertion: the source attributes this to the summary ("It says") and calls it reported experience. The title states it as an unattributed fact. Case: the summary says so, but some staff could not in fact see a waiting instrument, for example where a status was out of date. Vale's own remark shows how that could happen: "A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench." No supplied statement rules this out, and line 27 confirms that the claim is reported. | **Finding F1** |
| 2 | Deck: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs spent six weeks trialling a shared bench schedule." | "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "trial summary, dated 23 February 2026" | Time/completion: the source says a six-week trial *began*. It does not say that the trial ran for the full six weeks or when it ended. Case: the trial began on 26 January and the summary is dated 23 February, four weeks later, so six weeks had not been spent when the summary was written. Nothing supplied rules this out. | **Finding F2** |
| 3 | Deck: "Manager Priya Vale describes what the team had to settle first and what Vale would change" | "workshop manager Priya Vale"; Q: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?"; Q: "what would you change?" | 8 | Heading: "Fenwick defined its own job statuses" | "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices" | "own" reflects the contrast in the source: the workshop defined the statuses and Benchline configured them. "its": singular, non-personal. | Supported |
| 9 | "Benchline configured the workshop's choices, including who would update each status" | "decided who would update them. It is not attributed to Vale or to the trial, and it claims no result. The source says the material is not "a recommendation for every workshop". The closer is framed as an editorial starting point, not as a finding of the trial, so it is not a source-support defect. Editorial question only: the brief says no call to action is supplied, and whether this closer reads as one is for the editor. | Not a finding (editorial question) |

### Pronouns and gender
The draft uses no personal pronoun for Priya Vale. The name is repeated ("what Vale would change", "Vale approved", "Vale wrote"), so the draft asserts no natural gender, which matches the source. "we" and "I" appear only inside verbatim quotations. "its" and "it" refer to Fenwick, the team, Benchline or the summary: all third person singular and non-personal, matching the source's number. "your workshop" addresses the reader. No natural-gender assertion was found.

### Omissions that affect claims
None of the draft's claims loses a qualification that the source attaches. The body keeps the summary's non-measurement of duration, revenue and satisfaction.

**F1: the title drops the attribution to the summary.**
- Draft: "Fenwick staff could see which instruments awaited parts"
- Source: "It [the trial summary] says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience"
- Problem: the title turns something the workshop's summary reports into a fact asserted without attribution. Case: the summary says so, yet some staff could not see a waiting instrument, for example because a status had not been updated. Nothing supplied excludes this.
- Smallest repair: "Fenwick's trial summary says staff could see which instruments awaited parts". Alternative: "Fenwick's trial: staff report seeing which instruments awaited parts".

**F2: the deck turns a six-week trial that "began" into six weeks actually spent.**
- Draft: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs spent six weeks trialling a shared bench schedule."
- Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." The summary is dated 23 February 2026, and no end date is given.
- Problem: the source does not establish that the trial ran its full six weeks, or that six weeks had passed when the summary was written. Case: the trial began on 26 January and the summary followed four weeks later. Nothing supplied excludes this.
- Smallest repair: "In January 2026 Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." Alternatively, "Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial…".

## Translation findings
None. The source and the draft are both English, and the quotations are reproduced verbatim.

## Completion status
Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, deck, headings and body has been accounted for. Two unresolved source-support findings remain: F1 (unattributed title) and F2 (the deck's "spent six weeks"). One editorial question remains open, and it is not a defect: whether the closing advice reads as a call to action, given the brief.
